chapters.title: Chapter 2: The New Multipolar World: US, China, and the Rest

lessons.title: The US-China Rivalry: Trade Wars, Tariffs, and Tech Decoupling

body.text: The US-China rivalry is the single geopolitical axis that touches the most Indian portfolios at once, through IT services demand, electronics and API imports, and the metals and rare earths that sit inside almost everything you own.

children.text: Chapter 1 gave you the tools: the four channels, the power-resources-alliances framework, and how to read VIX and gold. This chapter applies those tools to the relationship that shapes more headlines, and more market moves, than any other in the current decade: the rivalry between the United States and China. It shows up as tariffs on goods, restrictions on chips, and, increasingly, a redrawing of where the world manufactures things, a redrawing India has a direct stake in.
From Trade War to Tech War: A Timeline

body.title: Key Moments in the US-China Rivalry

events.title: Trade war begins
events.description: The US imposed tariffs on hundreds of billions of dollars of Chinese goods, citing trade imbalances and intellectual property concerns. China retaliated with its own tariffs on US goods, mostly agricultural.

events.title: Phase One deal
events.description: The two countries signed a limited trade agreement in which China committed to increased purchases of US goods. Most existing tariffs stayed in place, this was a partial truce, not a resolution.

events.title: First major chip export controls
events.description: The US Commerce Department imposed sweeping restrictions on exporting advanced semiconductors and chipmaking equipment to China, marking the shift from a trade war to an explicit technology war.

events.title: China restricts gallium and germanium
events.description: Beijing announced export restrictions on gallium and germanium, critical inputs for chips and defence electronics, widely read as a direct retaliation to the chip controls.

events.title: Controls widen
events.description: The US tightened chip export rules further and expanded its Entity List of restricted Chinese firms, with allies including the Netherlands and Japan aligning parts of their own export rules.

events.title: Tariff escalation and a partial truce
events.description: A fresh round of sweeping US tariff increases in April 2025 was met with matching Chinese retaliation, pushing bilateral tariff rates to extreme levels within weeks, before both sides agreed to a temporary rollback in Geneva in May 2025 to allow further negotiation.

children.text: A tariff is simply a tax on imported goods, paid by the importer, not the exporting country's government. Its real-world effect depends on who ends up bearing that extra cost: an importer can absorb it and take a margin hit, pass it on to the end consumer through higher prices, or the exporter can lower its own price to stay competitive. In practice, the burden usually gets split three ways, which is exactly why tariffs are such a blunt tool, easy to announce, unpredictable in exactly who pays for them.

children.text: Tech Decoupling: Export Controls Cut Both Ways

Tariffs get the headlines, but export controls are the more surgical, and arguably more consequential, weapon in this rivalry. Each side controls something the other genuinely needs, and both have started using that leverage deliberately.

cells: Advanced semiconductors and the equipment used to manufacture them
Restrictions announced from October 2022, tightened in subsequent years, limiting China's access to the most advanced chip manufacturing capability
China's rare earth and mineral export restrictions
Materials essential to chips, magnets, and defence electronics
Export curbs on gallium and germanium announced in 2023, widely read as a direct response to US chip controls
Specific companies barred or restricted from receiving certain US technology
Chinese chipmakers and telecom equipment firms added over successive years
Where a country's own capital and expertise are allowed to flow
US restrictions on American investment into specific Chinese semiconductor and AI-related firms

body.label: China's Share of Global Rare Earth Processing
body.context: Even rare earths mined elsewhere are often sent to China for the specialised refining that turns raw ore into usable material, which is what makes China's export control lever so powerful

children.text: Why This Matters for Indian Investors

Indian portfolios connect to this rivalry through three separate threads. Indian IT services companies earn a large share of revenue from US and global clients, so a slowdown in global technology capital spending, whether from tariffs, uncertainty, or a broader risk-off mood, feeds directly into IT sector earnings and stock performance. Indian electronics manufacturers and pharmaceutical companies depend on China for components and active pharmaceutical ingredients, so export restrictions or supply disruptions there raise costs or create shortages here. And the flip side of decoupling is opportunity, as global companies look to diversify manufacturing away from China, India has been a direct beneficiary, a trend detailed in the next lesson.

body.title: A New Round of Chip Controls
body.scenario: The US announces a new round of restrictions on chip exports to China, broader than any previous round. Within days, China responds by tightening its own export rules on a critical mineral used in magnet manufacturing.
body.prompt: Name one Indian sector that could be hurt by this exchange, and one that could plausibly benefit, and explain your reasoning for each.
body.modelAnswer: Hurt: Indian electronics manufacturers that rely on the affected mineral for components could face higher input costs or supply delays, since China's restriction affects the material regardless of the final assembly location. Benefit: Indian IT hardware or component assembly players could gain over time if global companies accelerate diversifying supply chains away from China as a direct response to the intensifying restrictions, a shift examined more closely in the next lesson.

body.title: Tariffs vs Export Controls
body.question: What is the key difference between a tariff and an export control, as tools of geopolitical leverage?
options: A tariff is illegal under international law, while export controls are not
A tariff taxes goods coming in, while an export control restricts specific goods or technology from going out
They are two names for the same policy tool
Only export controls can be applied to a country's own companies
body.explanation: A tariff is a tax applied to imports entering a country. An export control restricts what a country allows to leave it, whether specific goods, technology, or investment. Both are used as geopolitical leverage, but they work in opposite directions.

cards.definition: A tax imposed on imported goods, paid by the importer in the country receiving them, not by the exporting country's government.
A US Commerce Department list of specific foreign companies and organisations restricted from receiving certain American technology and goods without a special licence.
Shifting supply chains toward politically aligned or trusted countries, rather than purely toward the lowest-cost location, as a way of reducing geopolitical risk.
Government review or restriction of a country's own companies and investors putting capital, or expertise, into specific foreign firms or sectors seen as sensitive.

points: The US-China rivalry escalated from a trade war centred on tariffs in 2018 into an explicit technology war from October 2022 onward, with export controls on chips and critical minerals as the main weapons

Tariff rates in this relationship have swung dramatically and quickly, including a spike above 100 percent and a partial rollback within weeks in 2025, making any specific figure a snapshot rather than a stable fact
Export controls cut both ways: the US restricts advanced chip technology, while China restricts rare earths and critical minerals, each side leveraging what the other genuinely needs
China processes the large majority of the world's rare earths even when mined elsewhere, which is what gives its export restrictions outsized leverage

Indian portfolios connect to this rivalry through IT services revenue tied to global tech spending, electronics and pharma input dependence on China, and the China Plus One manufacturing shift, covered in the next lesson
